problem.summary: In January the Governor’s Budget projected a $2.9 billion shortfall for 2026-27 and a deficit of roughly $22 billion in 2027-28. Higher revenue at the May Revision plus new revenue, spending reductions and fund shifts balanced both years; the Enacted Budget keeps that framework, ends 2026-27 with $4.5B in the SFEU and rebuilds the Rainy Day Fund to $15.1B.

quotes.text: The 2026 Budget Act largely maintains the May Revision framework, which balances the budget in both the 2026-27 and 2027-28 fiscal years, and significantly reduces the projected structural deficits in 2028-29 and 2029-30.
Further, the Budget includes a number of strategic investments, mostly one-time, that are possible in large part because of increased revenue since the 2025 Budget Act.
California is required to adopt a balanced budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year, measured by maintaining a positive balance in the state’s Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties (SFEU).
Established in 2024, the Surplus Holding Account allows the state to set aside a portion of anticipated surplus funds for allocation in a subsequent fiscal year.
As a result, the Budget does not include new significant spending proposals.

At the same time, however, constitutional funding requirements, the need for an adequate discretionary budget reserve, and higher program costs are additional commitments that exceed the level of increased revenues, resulting in a modest projected shortfall of $2.9 billion.

While the Budget is balanced in the 2026-27 fiscal year, with a discretionary reserve of $4.5 billion, it projects a deficit of roughly $22 billion in the 2027-28 fiscal year and shortfalls in the two years following.

The Budget forecast reflects General Fund revenues that are higher by more than $42 billion over the budget window, from 2024-25 through 2026-27, than projected at the 2025 Budget Act—an increase driven by higher cash receipts, higher stock market levels, and an improved economic outlook.
Estimated General Fund revenues from the Big Three sources (Personal Income, Corporate, and Sales and Use Taxes) are $16.5 billion higher than projected in January over the three-year budget window.
This is approximately $1.8 billion lower than estimated at the Governor’s Budget.
In January, the Governor’s Budget provided a plan to close a shortfall estimated at $2.9 billion in fiscal year 2026-27, ending with a discretionary reserve of $4.5 billion.
The 2025 Budget Act included numerous spending reductions that, at the time of enactment, were estimated to result in almost $12 billion in ongoing savings.
In responsibly balancing the budget over the next two fiscal years, the 2026 Budget Act includes SFEU balances of $4.5 billion in 2026-27 and $403 million in 2027-28.

To assist in providing for a positive SFEU in 2027-28 and more prudently manage the state’s resources, the Budget includes a transfer of $6.4 billion into the Projected Surplus Temporary Holding Account (Surplus Holding Account) in 2026-27.
However, the budget includes a $3.6 billion deposit into the BSA in 2026-27 and a minor “true-up” for the 2024-25 fiscal year.
As a result of the increase in revenue, the total suspension in 2025-26 is $5.4 billion.
Over the last two fiscal years, the state has withdrawn approximately $12.2 billion from the BSA and suspended deposits into the BSA for the 2024-25 and 2025-26 fiscal years.
After accounting for these actions, the BSA balance in 2026-27 is $15.1 billion—an increase of $3.9 billion compared to the 2025 Budget Act level of $11.2 billion.
In addition, the budget includes $4.5 billion in the SFEU and $9.2 billion in the Public School System Stabilization Account—bringing the combined reserves in 2026-27 to $28.8 billion.
When accounting for the balance in the Surplus Holding Account, the budget sets aside approximately $35.2 billion for future funding obligations in the 2026-27 fiscal year.
Revenue —$3.6 billion in total solutions in 2026-27 —growing to $5.1 billion in 2027-28 and decreasing slightly to $4.4 billion in 2029-30.
Spending Reductions and Reforms —$411 million in total solutions in 2026-27 — growing to $711.9 million by 2029-30.
General Fund Offsets —$390.7 million in total solutions in 2026-27 decreasing slightly to $256.5 million by 2029-30, including:

Managed Care Organization (MCO) Tax —The Budget reflects the renewal of a House of Representatives (H.R.) 1 compliant MCO Tax, effective January 1, 2027, increasing revenue by a projected $575 million in 2026-27, $2.3 billion in 2027-28 and 2028-29, and $1.7 billion in 2029-30, to support the Medi-Cal program and maintain targeted rate increases for primary, maternal, and non-specialty mental health care.
The limitation is projected to increase General Fund revenue by $1 billion in 2026-27, $3.3 billion in 2027-28, $4.7 billion in 2028-29, and $4.2 billion in 2029-30.
This is projected to increase General Fund revenue by $450 million in 2026-27 and $900 million in 2027-28 and annually thereafter.

differences.title: Transfers & loans move money between funds
differences.body: Schedule 8 lists General Fund revenue of $237.4B before transfers. Net transfers and loans of −$10.6B — mostly deposits into reserve accounts that are legally separate funds — bring “revenues and transfers” to $226.8B. Across all state funds the transfers net to almost nothing (−$0.35B): what leaves the General Fund shows up as special-fund revenue.

DOF Summary Schedule 10 — Summary of Fund Condition Statements (Enacted)

differences.title: Spending is partly paid from last year’s balance
differences.body: The General Fund starts 2026-27 with $57.2B carried in: $28.0B already committed (encumbrances) and $29.2B in the discretionary reserve, built up as revenue ran more than $42 billion above the 2025 Budget Act forecast from 2024-25 through 2026-27 (Governor’s Budget estimate). Spending of $251.5B exceeds revenues and transfers by $24.7B, and that gap is covered by drawing the balance down to $32.5B. The State measures a balanced budget by a positive SFEU at year end ($4.5B), so a planned draw on the carry-in is consistent with a balanced budget.

differences.title: Reserves sit outside the General Fund
differences.body: The Rainy Day Fund ($15.1B), the school reserve ($9.2B) and the Surplus Holding Account ($6.4B) are special funds. A deposit is a General Fund transfer out (it lowers “revenues and transfers”) and special-fund revenue in, so it inflates special-fund revenue ($101.7B) and balances ($52.9B, of which $30.7B are these reserves).

differences.title: Not all of the fund balance is available
differences.body: Of the $32.5B General Fund ending balance, $28.0B is the Reserve for Liquidation of Encumbrances — money already committed to contracts and orders not yet paid (an accrual/timing item under GAAP). Only the SFEU ($4.5B) is a true discretionary reserve.

differences.title: Federal funds and bonds aren’t state revenue
differences.body: $187.2B of federal funds and $5.1B of bond-financed spending are in total spending but not in Schedule 8 revenue: federal grants arrive for specific programs and bond proceeds are borrowing, repaid later through General Fund debt service.

differences.title: “All funds” counts some dollars twice
differences.body: ebudget’s $793.7B “all funds” figure adds $45.5B of reimbursements (one department paying another — already counted where the money started) and $209.2B of nongovernmental cost funds (pension trusts, university own funds, local property tax and similar pass-throughs). This explorer leaves both out, so total spending is $538.9B (state $351.7B + federal $187.2B).

differences.title: Budget basis isn’t accounting basis
differences.body: Budget-year and current-year figures are estimates. Schedule 1 notes that the encumbrance reserve follows Generally Accepted Accounting Principles and Government Code sections 13306–13307, but the budget is a plan, not an audit: actual results are reported later (the past-year column already reflects them) and accrual and timing adjustments mean the State’s audited financial statements will not match these figures exactly.

differences.title: Thousands vs. millions vs. billions
differences.body: Schedules print thousands of dollars; Summary Charts print millions; the narrative rounds to tenths of a billion. Each rounding step can shift a total by a few units — e.g. the Introduction’s “$28.8 billion” combined reserves is the rounded sum of three schedule lines. Every figure on this page is checked against its source within the rounding of the printed unit.

notes: Amounts are in thousands of dollars as printed in DOF Summary Schedules; narrative figures are converted from “$X billion/million”.
Figures marked “transcribed” come from Summary Charts printed as images and were keyed by hand (millions); each is cross-checked against Schedule 1 where both exist.

Transfers to the BSA, Safety Net Reserve and Surplus Holding Account are taken from those funds’ Schedule 10 rows (revenues = transfers in); “other transfers” is the remainder of Schedule 8 net transfers & loans.
Check status: “ties” = within tolerance; “explained” = the sources genuinely differ and documented, cited causes account for the whole difference; “differs” = unexplained.

Explorer spending excludes fund 0201 Medical Providers Interim Payment Fund (Health Care Services; ebudget class “federal”): it is financed by General Fund / Federal Trust Fund loans and its expenditures are moved to the regular Budget Act items (Gov. Code 16531.1; DOF Manual of State Funds, fund 0201), and Schedule 9 does not count it.
